newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols slide but focus stays on stocks.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols slide but focus stays on stocks.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options slipped on Thursday as the U.S. dollar ground higher, but dealers said nervousness about the state of the U.S. stock market continued to lend support to levels.
"There's not so much fear about the dollar downside although people are still a little skittish about the stock market," said one over-the-counter dealer with a U.S. firm.
"If we get another big move in the stock market, that will have a big effect (on volatilities)," he said.
At 1245 CST/1845 GMT, dealers quoted implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark options at 8.3 percent compared with 8.7 percent late Wednesday.
Implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen at-the-money options was seen at 7.05 percent compared with 7.35 percent.

One dealer noted heavy interest in the morning to hedge currencies against a tightening of rates by the Federal Reserve. However, after the release of U.S. retail sales and consumer price data for November, those fears eased.
The consumer price index was in line with expectations, showing a rise of 0.3 percent.
However, November retail sales fell 0.4 percent, catching the market by surprise.
The data made it appear less likely the Fed will be tempted to hike rates, which also contributed to the drop in volatility, he said.
Next week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting will keep levels from dropping much further, another dealer predicted.
Weakness in the U.S. stock markets was having little impact on front-dated volatility on Thursday, but players remain jittery about the potential for a steep slide, he said.

"Dollar/mark and dollar/yen have been pretty well behaved," he said. "Last Friday (the drop in stocks) affected all the markets simultaneously, whereas this time around it seems to have left the currency markets pretty much alone. But that surely will still be a major factor going forward."
Nervousness about stocks may have contributed to high volatilities further out on the curve, he said.
"The front-end vol curves are more or less fair value. But the back end is still quite high," he said.
In contrast, nothing appeared to be worrying currency futures options, according to traders at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange's IMM.
Implied volatilities were flat to softer, trade was extremely thin, and there appeared to be little concern about the state of the U.S. stock or bond futures markets, one trader said.
"We're absolutely dead. This is the quietest it's been in probably two months," he said.
